body.text: What has deeply undermined these accusations is that Yogi Adityanath, the powerful BJP chief minister of Uttar Pradesh, too is concerned with the effects of the SIR in his state – on Hindu voters. Not to mention the Delhi SIR earlier this year, which led to prominent BJP politicians, including India’s foreign minister and Delhi’s chief minister, being flagged as discrepant cases.
In other words, with a healthy nod to Hanlon’s razor, the SIR mess points to something more pedestrian: the use of extremely glitchy and poorly designed software.

An equally mundane explanation, for last week’s cyber outages, has emerged: Much of the software that serves as the backbone of daily life and governance remains ridden with bugs that are only now coming to light thanks to the stupendous ability of frontier AI models to identify vulnerabilities and the concomitant fear of hackers exploiting them. The outages were unexpected outcomes of the rush to fix these bugs, it turns out, as opposed to a large-scale cyber attack by hostile actors or AI agent swarms.
These make for psychologically unsatisfactory explanations all the same.

After all, it is a little outlandish to imagine that the NSA – perhaps one of the world’s most tech-savvy organisations – uses software that “wasn’t designed, [but] evolved” (as one former NSA officialput it), a sprawling monster that earns its keep simply because it's too expensive to get rid of. Or that American civil aviation was essentially held hostage by router maintenance in a small Arkansas town.

Similarly, it is hard to believe that the world’s largest democracy uses a software system that generates red flags because it can’t process data from twins. (The SIR software rules apparently require a nine-month gap between siblings as one of the consistency conditions to prevent voter misrepresentation.) Or that other electoral software would merrily accept manifestly made-up voter names, as was the case ahead of local elections in an Uttar Pradesh constituency last month.

One reason why we instinctively reject the possibility that the world is awash with badly designed and brittle code is how the tech industry has – over the past two decades or so, the Era of the Apple as it were – tried to design consumer software that looks and feels slick. This concerted attempt to reduce “friction” has meant that the overwhelming majority sees very little of how these things work – just that they do, at least most of the time.

The science fiction writer Arthur C. Clarke famously noted that “[a]ny sufficiently advanced technology is indistinguishable from magic”. Technologists however worry about societies that are all too happy to club boon-granting deities and the latest cell phone model in the same mental box.
Such societies are fertile ground for conspiracism.

The Republican senator Josh Hawley all but suggested that last week’s outages were linked, with slender evidence. US President Donald Trump’s former national security adviser Michael Flynn claimed that they were part of a cyber-attack, again on the basis of nothing more than a hunch. It didn’t help that the Trump administration’s messaging on the outages were uneven, paving the way for myriad social media conspiracies. Ironically, its decision to fire the White House cyber chief over the outages is likely to be viewed as government cover-up by those who had already made up their minds. Meanwhile, the outages led to a spike in panic-buying across the Atlantic, in the United Kingdom amid an unrelated standing emergency-preparedness government advisory.

In India, opposition leader Rahul Gandhi continues to repeat his allegations, even as he coyly sidesteps the question of why his party is not boycotting elections if they are true. At the same time, serious investigative reporting has indicated that all is not exactly well within the election commission, even as the Modi government struggles to clear the air on potential problems in the commission’s software. None of this vindicates the opposition, but equally, continues to confuse many.
A wider conversation around the trade-offs (and not simply the gains) involved in large-scale digitisation could go a long way in assuring the public.
